elements.quote: Registration PROSPERO registration ID CRD42020193692.

elements.quote:
Previous studies have identified diabetes as an independent risk factor for poor prognosis of coronavirus ● disease-2019 (COVID-19)
...
However, some of the findings are still conflicting, imprecisely estimated or affected by risk of bias, such as confounding.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge (diabetes as a risk factor) and highlights important uncertainties including conflicting findings, imprecision, and risk of bias in existing studies.

elements.quote: To provide the best available evidence for the identification of risk phenotypes of diabetes in association with COVID-19 severity and death, a systematic review and meta-analysis is needed that summarises the findings, reveals more robust estimates, considers risk of bias and evaluates the certainty of evidence.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly explain the importance and need for conducting this systematic review and meta-analysis to summarise findings, obtain more robust estimates, consider risk of bias, and evaluate certainty of evidence.

elements.quote:
Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses on diabetes and COVID19 prognosis have observed an approximately two- to threefold increased risk of mortality due to COVID-19 for people with diabetes compared with people without diabetes [6 - 14].
...
Therefore, we are conducting a living systematic review and meta-analysis on the associations between phenotypes of diabetes and confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection with relation to COVID-19 death and severity.
elements.reason: The manuscript acknowledges existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses and explains the rationale and need for the current (living) review in that context.
The review concerns prognostic associations of diabetes phenotypes with COVID-19 outcomes, not effects of interventions; no mechanism of action of an intervention is relevant or described.
The review does not address complex interventions or delivery contexts and does not present or require a logic model; this reporting item is not applicable.

elements.quote: The aim of this study is to identify high-risk phenotypes of diabetes associated with COVID-19 severity and death.
elements.reason: The manuscript gives an explicit statement of the objective of the review (to identify high‑risk diabetes phenotypes associated with COVID‑19 severity and death).

elements.quote: This is the first edition of a living systematic review and meta-analysis on observational studies investigating phenotypes in individuals with diabetes and COVID-19-related death and severity.
elements.reason: The conditional item applies to reviews of intervention effects (PICO); this review synthesises observational studies of phenotypes, not intervention comparisons, so PICO-style planned comparisons are not applicable.

elements.quote: We included studies of any design that reported risk estimates (HR, RR or OR with 95% CI) for associations between phenotypes (general characteristics of individuals, diabetes-specific characteristics, presence of diabetes-related complications or underlying comorbidities, and laboratory parameters) and death and severity of COVID-19 in individuals with diabetes and WHO-defined confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection [20].
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies population, eligible study designs (any design), exposures and outcomes, but does not specify eligibility regarding study settings or any required follow-up periods; thus some required study characteristic details are missing.

elements.quote: Studies without primary clinical data (including modelling studies), editorials, letters, commentaries, reviews, articles not in English and guidelines were excluded.
elements.reason: Language restriction (articles not in English excluded) and exclusion of non-primary clinical data are specified, but other report characteristics such as dissemination year or explicit publication/report status criteria are not fully described (although search date is provided elsewhere), so reporting is partial.

elements.quote: No risk estimates
elements.reason: The study's flow chart of excluded full-text articles lists specific exclusion reasons including 'No risk estimates', distinguishing exclusion for missing outcome reporting from other exclusion reasons.

elements.quote: For similar exposures (with similar reference groups [e.g., men vs women; obese vs normal weight; use of insulin: yes vs no; pre-existing comorbidities: yes vs no]), meta-analyses were conducted separately for the two outcomes: death and severity.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies how studies were grouped for synthesis (examples of reference groups) and that meta-analyses were conducted separately for the two outcomes, linking groups to the review comparisons.

No rationale is provided in the retrieved evidence for notable eligibility restrictions (e.g., the reason for excluding non-English articles or other exclusions); the manuscript lists exclusions but does not explain the justification for these restrictions.

elements.quote: The literature search was conducted from inception up to 14 August 2020 by using predefined search terms (see electronic supplementary material (ESM) Table 1). ... The last update was on 10 October 2020.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the dates the searches covered (up to 14 August 2020) and the date of the last update (10 October 2020).

elements.quote: We searched PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih. gov), Web of Science (www.webofknowledge.com), Epistemonikos (www.epistemonikos.org) and the COVID19 Research Database (WHO) (https://search.bvsalud.org/ global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov). The literature search was conducted from inception up to 14 August 2020 ... The last update was on 10 October 2020.
elements.reason: Names and URLs of bibliographic databases/search platforms are reported and overall search date ranges are given, but the manuscript does not report the specific search interface/platform details per database beyond the URLs nor database-specific coverage dates.

elements.quote: We searched ... the COVID19 Research Database (WHO) (https://search.bvsalud.org/ global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov). The literature search was conducted from inception up to 14 August 2020 ... The last update was on 10 October 2020.
elements.reason: A study register/online repository (COVID19 Research Database (WHO)) is named with a URL and overall search dates are provided, but no register-specific date restrictions or coverage dates are reported.

elements.quote: We searched PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih. gov), Web of Science (www.webofknowledge.com), Epistemonikos (www.epistemonikos.org) and the COVID19 Research Database (WHO) (https://search.bvsalud.org/ global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov).

elements.quote: The screening of the studies was performed by two independent researchers (AL, MN) and any discrepancies were resolved by discussion with two other researchers (CH, SS). Titles and abstracts were scanned according to the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria (see below) and potentially relevant full texts were assessed for eligibility.

elements.quote: We included studies of any design that reported risk estimates (HR, RR or OR with 95% CI) for associations between phenotypes (general characteristics of individuals, diabetes-specific characteristics, presence of diabetes-related complications or underlying comorbidities, and laboratory parameters) and death and severity of COVID-19 in individuals with diabetes and WHO-defined confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection [20]. Severity of COVID-19 was defined as a composite endpoint, including death, endotracheal intubation for mechanical ventilation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, ICU admission, multiple organ dysfunction or failure, or hospital admission.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists and defines the outcome domains sought (death and severity) and provides a clear definition of 'severity' as a composite endpoint, and enumerates the phenotype domains considered.

elements.quote: Study design; follow-up ... Retrospective study; ND Retrospective study; 30 days ... Prospective study; 7 days ... Retrospective study; 28 days ...
elements.reason: Some included-study follow-up periods are reported in the study characteristics table (varying follow-up lengths for individual studies), but the review does not specify a consistent time frame of measurement for each outcome domain across studies or a prespecified time windows for outcomes in the Methods.

The manuscript does not state whether all results compatible with each outcome domain in each study were sought (e.g. all measures, time points, analyses); no explicit statement about seeking all compatible outcome results was found in the provided evidence.

As the authors of one report did not reply to our request [28], we assumed that in statistical analyses of continuous measures, the variable was investigated as per 1 unit increase.
elements.reason: When multiple reports from the same cohort were identified the authors describe selecting the study with the largest number of cases; they also describe an assumption applied when authors did not respond about continuous measures—this describes processes used to select/handle results.
No evidence was found in the provided material reporting changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or their importance, nor rationales for such changes.
No evidence was found describing changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains or rationales for such changes.

elements.quote: The aim of this study is to identify high-risk phenotypes of diabetes associated with COVID-19 severity and death. Methods This is the first edition of a living systematic review and meta-analysis on observational studies investigating phenotypes in individuals with diabetes and COVID-19-related death and severity.
elements.reason: The review explicitly focuses on death and severity as the principal outcomes for interpretation (stated as the aim), indicating these were the most important outcomes; however, the authors do not provide an explicit rationale for prioritising these outcomes beyond the stated aim.

elements.quote:
We included studies of any design that reported risk estimates (HR, RR or OR with 95% CI) for associations between phenotypes (general characteristics of individuals, diabetes-specific characteristics, presence of diabetes-related complications or underlying comorbidities, and laboratory parameters) and death and severity of COVID-19 in individuals with diabetes and WHO-defined confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection [20].

The extracted data of interest are listed in ESM Table 2.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the categories of phenotypes/variables sought (general characteristics, diabetes-specific characteristics, complications/comorbidities, laboratory parameters) and refers to a detailed extracted data list (ESM Table 2). Additionally, Results tables (table_2/table_3) show specific variables collected (age/sex, diabetes type, comorbidities, medication use, laboratory markers, outcome, study design, setting).

elements.quote: We successfully contacted study authors and received missing data or corrections for implausible data [16, 17, 24 - 27] and, thus, no study had to be excluded due to missing data. As the authors of one report did not reply to our request [28], we assumed that in statistical analyses of continuous measures, the variable was investigated as per 1 unit increase.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes actions taken for missing data (contacting authors and receiving data) and explicitly states an assumption made for one non-responding study (assuming continuous measures were per 1 unit increase).

elements.quote: The extracted data of interest are listed in ESM Table 2.
elements.reason: No citation or reference to a specific tool used to determine which data items to collect is provided. The text mentions a 'pre-piloted form' for data extraction but does not cite or identify a formal tool that determined the data items.

elements.quote:
Data analysis

For similar exposures (with similar reference groups [e.g., men vs women; obese vs normal weight; use of insulin: yes vs no; pre-existing comorbidities: yes vs no]), meta-analyses were conducted separately for the two outcomes: death and severity. We calculated summary RRs (SRR) and 95% CIs using DerSimonian and Laird random effects models and I 2 statistic to assess statistical heterogeneity.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the effect measure used for pooled analyses: summary relative risks (SRR) with 95% CIs and the random-effects model used to calculate them.

elements.quote: older age (>65 years) was associated with higher risk of COVID-19-related death (SRR 3.49 [95% CI 1.82, 6.69]; n = 6 studies ...). The strongest associations were observed for blood glucose levels >11 mmol/l at admission and death (SRR 8.60 [95% CI 2.25, 32.83]; n =2 studies; moderate certainty of evidence).
elements.reason: The manuscript reports specific thresholds used in analyses (e.g. age >65 years; blood glucose >11 mmol/l) and reports effect estimates for these ranges, but it does not provide a rationale or justification for the chosen thresholds or a general discussion of thresholds/ranges used to interpret effect size.
No description is provided of methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure (e.g., converting ORs to RRs) in the retrieved evidence.
The manuscript states the effect measure used (SRR) but does not provide a justification for the choice of this effect measure in the retrieved text.

elements.quote: For similar exposures (with similar reference groups [e.g., men vs women; obese vs normal weight; use of insulin: yes vs no; pre-existing comorbidities: yes vs no]), meta-analyses were conducted separately for the two outcomes: death and severity.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the process used to decide which studies were eligible for each synthesis: studies with similar exposures and reference groups were grouped and meta-analysed separately for the two outcomes (death and severity). Additional selection rules (inclusion criteria, study types, handling of duplicate cohorts) are also described elsewhere in the methods, supporting that study eligibility for syntheses was defined and applied.

elements.quote: We successfully contacted study authors and received missing data or corrections for implausible data [16, 17, 24 - 27] and, thus, no study had to be excluded due to missing data. As the authors of one report did not reply to our request [28], we assumed that in statistical analyses of continuous measures, the variable was investigated as per 1 unit increase.
elements.reason: The authors describe procedures to obtain missing data (contacting study authors and receiving missing data or corrections) and state a specific assumption used to handle missing information for one study (assuming continuous measures were per 1 unit increase), which are methods to prepare data for synthesis.

elements.quote: The characteristics of the studies are shown in Table 1 and more detailed information about the setting, the identified exposures and considered confounders in each study is shown in ESM Table 5. The extracted data of interest are listed in ESM Table 2.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states which tables present study characteristics and that extracted data items are listed in an electronic supplementary table, describing the tabular structures and the data included.

elements.quote: Publication bias was assessed by visual inspection of the funnel plots and applying Egger ' s test if more than ten studies were identified for one association [30].
elements.reason: The Methods describe graphical methods used to display results (funnel plots for publication bias); figures (Figs 2, 3) are also referenced for result presentation.

elements.quote: To explore the influence of potential confounding, we conducted stratified analysis by adjustment for important confounders (low/moderate risk vs high risk of bias in the confounding domain of the QUIPS tool). For similar exposures ... meta-analyses were conducted separately for the two outcomes: death and severity.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the basis for grouping/stratifying studies in analyses and figures (by outcome: death vs severity; and by risk-of-bias/adjustment categories).
No methods or rationale for use of non-standard (uncommon) graphs are described, and there is no evidence in the provided text that non-standard graphs were used.

elements.quote: All statistical analyses were conducted with Stata software version 15.1 (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX, USA).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the software and version used for statistical synthesis (Stata 15.1).
No description or justification of alternative synthesis or summary methods when meta-analysis was not possible is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We calculated summary RRs (SRR) and 95% CIs using DerSimonian and Laird random effects models
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the meta-analysis model (DerSimonian and Laird random-effects) used for each pooled analysis.

elements.quote: We calculated summary RRs (SRR) and 95% CIs using DerSimonian and Laird random effects models and I 2 statistic to assess statistical heterogeneity. Publication bias was assessed by visual inspection of the funnel plots and applying Egger ' s test if more than ten studies were identified for one association [30].
elements.reason: The statistical methods for synthesis are described including calculation of summary RRs, 95% CIs, heterogeneity assessment, and publication bias testing.

elements.quote: I 2 statistic to assess statistical heterogeneity. Publication bias was assessed by visual inspection of the funnel plots and applying Egger ' s test if more than ten studies were identified for one association [30].

Most of the studies ( n = 14) were conducted in Asia (China, n = 8; South Korea, n = 3; Singapore, n = 1; Iran, n = 1; Israel n = 1), whilst five studies were conducted in North America (USA, n = 4; Mexico, n = 1) and three studies in Europe (France, n = 1; Fig. 1 Flow chart of the literature search Italy, n = 1; Spain, n = 1). elements.quote: Older age, male sex, obesity, hypertension, chronic pulmonary diseases, CVD, active cancer [3 - 6, 21], laboratory parameters (e.g. low lymphocyte count, and elevations in CRP, ALT and AST) [48] have been linked to a poor prognosis of COVID-19 in the general population infected with SARS-CoV-2. These risk factors among the general population are in line with the risk factors we identified in the diabetes populations, with some exceptions. Interestingly, we did not observe a positive association for obesity or hypertension with COVID-19 severity or death in people with diabetes and COVID-19. ... Interestingly, findings from a large representative study in England indicated that higher HbA1c was associated with poor prognosis of COVID-19 in individuals with diabetes: the RR (95% CI) for HbA1c < 7.5% (<58.5 mmol/mol) and death was 1.31 (1.24, 1.37), and for HbA1c ≥ 7.5% ( ≥ 58.5 mmol/mol), it was 1.95 (1.83, 2.08) compared with individuals without diabetes [20]. ... After our last update, eligible studies providing important data have been published on this topic, such as the report from McGurnaghan et al., which covered the whole Scottish population, including individuals with diabetes [50]. In general, the data support our findings but provide new insights on further risk factors not included in our study.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the review's findings with evidence from the general population and recent large population studies (England, Scotland), notes consistencies and differences (e.g., obesity and hypertension), and places the results within the broader evidence base.

elements.quote: Our study has a number of limitations. First, there was a low number of primary studies for some of the associations assessed, including diabetes-specific factors (e.g. diabetes duration, HbA1c, use of specific glucose-lowering medications), certain comorbidities (e.g. cancer, liver disease, and dementia) and laboratory parameters at admission (e.g. CRP, differential blood cell count, liver enzymes). For these associations, the certainty of evidence was mainly graded as low or very low, reflecting that future research might change the findings. Second, the risk of bias was high for eight studies (36% of the studies included), mainly due to insufficient adjustment of important confounders. However, we stratified our meta-analyses by risk of bias due to confounding and the overall findings were robust, with two exceptions; older age and CKD were more strongly associated with COVID-19related death in studies with high risk of bias compared with studies with low or moderate risk of bias due to confounding. Third, it was not possible to conduct stratified analyses by study design, data collection and diabetes type. Fourth, the primary studies did not account for possible specific treatment of COVID-19. Fifth, a general question remains as to whether deceased participants died with or due to COVID-19. Finally, these findings cannot be generalised to all individuals with diabetes infected with SARS-CoV-2 because only individuals with the more severe form of COVID-19 are included in the primary studies and the majority of the studies were conducted in the hospital setting.
elements.reason: The Discussion section explicitly lists and discusses multiple limitations of the included evidence (low number of primary studies for some associations, low certainty, high risk of bias in several studies, inability to stratify by design/type, lack of COVID-19 treatment data, uncertainty about cause of death, limited generalisability).
